name: Freya Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play accordion at two community dance nights, record plain practice tunes and help a senior tutor show adults the first buttons. I spent thirty years in a hotel kitchen, finished secondary school, and only started being paid for music four years ago. I still follow the lead player.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does that work mean in your household now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner and I have grown children, but the bills are ours. At 58, I can see retirement coming without knowing what it will pay; our savings cover about three weeks, and junior music fees are low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the dance organiser that a quicker poster is useful, but people still need someone to keep the tune moving. I would ask for the fee before packing my accordion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three weeks saved will not cover a cancelled dance month. There are few paid accordion seats nearby, so ordinary gaps already worry me even if AI does little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would keep the two paid dance nights, recorded practice tunes and supervised adult lessons. I would ask the organiser for the next three dates and cancellation payment in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel anxious about the existing gaps. A calm technology story does not fill an empty Saturday envelope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Was a dance cancelled recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The winter hall flooded and the organiser paid half our fee. I would ask for the other half in the next written agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children cover a missing fee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have families of their own. I might accept a lift, but I would not write their wages into our budget.

I would ask for the **dance fee** before packing my accordion.
think: Our **three-week reserve** cannot carry a month without paid dances.
Few **local accordion posts** offer a quick replacement.
do: Keep **paid dance nights**, recordings and supervised lessons this month.
Request **written dates** and cancellation pay before the next dance agreement.
feel: I feel **anxious** about existing fee gaps.
S0.quote: A calm technology story does not fill an empty Saturday envelope.
fieldNote: Her **hotel-kitchen past** explains a junior music start at 58 and why she still relies on a supervising player.
Her **thin cushion** makes ordinary hall cancellations a current income risk.

steps.text: Keep paid accordion dances, practice recordings and supervised adult lessons
Request written dance dates and full cancellation fee before next agreement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the organiser that cheap generated practice tunes may help beginners, but a paid tutor still has to watch their hands. I would ask the organiser to keep my lesson-assistant hours on the schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Recorded tunes make up about a fifth of my low pay, and software could take that small commission. I cannot simply call myself an expert teacher to replace it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would show the organiser the practice-tune invoices and request written paid assistant hours. In the first year, if recording fees fall, I would keep the paid dances and seek a posted adult-music aide role only if my secondary schooling and supervised experience qualify, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the bus timetable works; I would stay until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the tune fees. I have never used AI, and I would rather keep a paid lesson than buy a machine I do not understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the new music-making app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the organiser paid for instruction, approved local storage and let the senior tutor check a nameless tune I own by ear. I would stop if the tune changed or left the centre, but I am not agreeing to test it now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if someone tells you a tutor job may open?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the dances. A spoken possibility is not a posted paid vacancy with written hours.

say: I would defend **paid lesson assistance** with the organiser.
I would explain **live hand guidance** still matters to adult beginners.
think: Generated **practice tunes** could remove a fifth of my pay.
My **junior teaching skill** cannot replace those fees alone.
do: Show **tune invoices** and request written paid assistant hours next month.
Apply for **posted music aide** after lost fees only if qualified; written net after travel replaces fees, bus works.
Keep **paid dance nights** until a suitable signed offer states hours.
feel: I feel **anxious** about lost tune fees.
S1.quote: I would rather keep a paid lesson than buy a machine I do not understand.
fieldNote: Her **untried app conditions** do not amount to an actual learn-AI plan.
The **aide move** needs lost fees, qualification, a posted paid role, written net replacement and transport.

steps.text: Request written paid music-assistant hours after showing practice-tune invoices
Apply for secondary/experience-qualified posted aide after fee loss; written net after travel replaces fees, bus fits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the dance hall that AGI by 2028 may make practice tunes instantly. I would ask which live nights and lesson hours still have signed fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect tune commissions to stop in 2028, and I fear the organiser may buy fewer paid dance nights. Robots that can play the accordion come around 2031, three years later. My recording wage is at risk before accordion-playing robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would count tune invoices and request a signed paid dance calendar. In the first year after 2028, if live dance fees also fall, I would apply for a posted centre music-room aide role only if my schooling and supervised lesson experience qualify, written net pay after travel covers lost dance fees and the bus gets me home; I would keep paid lessons and dances until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about likely tune losses; I would be alarmed if dances also went, taking most of my wage. I have stayed awake adding three weeks of savings against the next rent bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a teaching course now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a real posted job requires it and funding or paid study hours exist. I cannot borrow against a class that may not hire me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire at 60 instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 60 in 2028, but I have no written retirement estimate yet. I would request one while keeping paid work.

I would ask which **live nights and lessons** retain signed fees.

do: Count **tune invoices** and request a signed paid dance calendar now.
Apply for **posted music aide** after 2028 dance cuts if qualified; written net after travel covers fees, bus fits.
Keep **paid lessons and dances** until signed offer; request retirement estimate; take posted-job-required course only with funded tuition or paid study hours.
feel: I feel **anxious** about likely tune losses; losing dances too would alarm me.
S2.quote: My recording wage is at risk before accordion-playing robots arrive.
fieldNote: Her **2028 recording loss** precedes capable accordion robots around 2031.
The **centre move** needs actual dance cuts, posted qualification, written net pay, workable bus and signed offer.

steps.text: Count paid tune invoices and request signed dance calendar now
Apply for secondary/experience-qualified posted aide after dance cuts; written net after travel covers fees, bus fits
Keep paid lessons/dances until signed offer; request written retirement estimate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the organiser that five years until AGI by 2031 is time to find out whether neighbours will pay for a small dance class. I would not ask the lead player to teach for a smile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Practice recordings may stop paying by 2031, and accordion robots could arrive around 2034. A paid group might replace the tune fees, but I cannot fund a hall myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This autumn I would help run a six-week beginner dance-music group only if the lead player agrees to supervise, the hall commits a room and hire fee in writing before deposits, and eight adults prepay enough for rent, safe loan accordions, the lead player’s wage and my teaching and preparation. In the first year after 2031 I would repeat only while those eight fees cover both wages including my preparation, the room and checked instruments; otherwise I would keep the paid lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious until the numbers pay both of us. Three weeks of savings are not a budget for the beginner dance-music group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who checks the loan accordions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall caretaker must inspect straps and cases before anyone lifts one. If a loan instrument fails, the learner brings a safe one or I cancel that place. If a cancellation leaves fewer than eight paid places, I would find a replacement or defer and refund the group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only four adults pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would refund all four. Their money will not cover the hall, lead player and my preparation.

Repeat the **paid group** after 2031 only while eight fees cover wages, preparation, written room and inspected instruments.

feel: I feel **anxious** because savings cannot finance a room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the dance hall that a decade until AGI by 2036 is time to write down fees and train the next player properly. At 68 I may still need a paid Saturday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tune fees may end by 2036 and robots may play dances around 2039. My small savings and low junior rate are a problem this year, even with a long warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this term I would ask for a two-year written paid dance agreement and save five percent of each extra paid wedding tune after rent, food and bus fare, aiming for two months. In the first year after 2036 I would keep paid lessons and, only if dance or tune fees fall, apply for a posted community-centre music aide role only if my schooling qualifies, written net pay after travel covers lost dance and tune fees and the bus works; I would leave only after a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay anxious about getting through the next winter. Ten years to prepare does not give me ten years of wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no weddings book?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I save nothing new from that source. I will not call an empty calendar a savings plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you know what retirement will pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would request a written estimate and keep working until I know what is real.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because tune fees and paid dances might both fall. Signed dance dates, a qualified posted aide job with written pay and a bus home would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the older lead player when the class ends. A neighbour’s smile is welcome, but it is not a second wage.

headlineQuote: A neighbour’s smile is welcome, but it is not a second wage.
portrait: At **58**, Freya is a junior accordionist who left hotel kitchen work and completed secondary school.
Her **lower pay**, three-week reserve and few local jobs make cancelled dances an immediate risk.
She has **never used AI** and would only consider a tool after paid instruction, privacy approval and senior checks.
A **paid beginner group** requires a supervising lead, eight prepaid adults, safe accordions, room and both wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase tune fees and cut paid dance nights before a new job appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed dance dates**, a qualified posted aide job with written net pay and workable bus service would help Freya.
